doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Her sister's band and learning bass on a three-string school bass
summary: Her sister collected records and formed a band needing a bass player; Nicki taught herself on a school bass, and recalls a pre-computer childhood full of bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And your sister was sort of preceding you in this musical endeavor?

Yes. She also played piano and clarinet and tenor sax, and she got some records around then. I was 14, she was 16, something like that. And she came home with all these records, Charlie Parker, Louis Armstrong, everything. I don’t even know how she got half these records but she came home with all these records, and then she formed a band, right? You’ve probably heard this story.

Yeah. She formed a band, and she said, “I don’t need a flute player in my band.” And I looked up to her so much back then, and I still do, you know, she’s always been a good musician, my sister, you know what I mean? She’s always had her own mind, her own sound, really her own voice from a young age. I really feel that about her. She’s just full of her own ambition musically, throughout her life. Very interesting. And so like okay. But there was a bass at school. And she said, “Do you want to be in my band, I need a bass player.” So lo and behold there was a bass at school and a guy across the road that kind of played bass in a Dixieland band in Newcastle, with three strings. It didn’t even have four strings on it. He says no one hears the bottom string, don’t worry about it, just three strings are enough.
Yeah. So I was set up with the bass and I kind of taught myself. Because I didn’t know he teaches in Newcastle at the time.
That’s interesting how those little things happen in your life that send you in a certain direction for almost ever. You know, like your sister saying, “Well I need a bass player.”

Yeah it is bizarre. It is bizarre. But when you’re young and you’ve got the time, you know what I mean, you’ve got the time to just search things out. In the pre-computer age. Do you know what I mean? I was of the generation that computers were brought into the high school but they weren’t taken seriously. They were like well we really don’t have enough computers for you to take computer class. Oh okay. So I was that transition kid where it was the start of the technological age but not really embraced yet, you know what I mean? So we had oodles of time to practice, to do athletics, practice after school activities, school band, concert band, local bands, you name it. We were in everything. The Marching Koalas.
